messages.subject: Looking for alternative explanations that we may have missed
messages.subject_clean: Looking for alternative explanations that we may have missed
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I wanted to reach out to the group to get fresh eyes and opinions regarding the results from our overwintering origin study. We’ve used δ2H to determine the natal origin of captured corn earworm (CEW) moths. We are skeptical that some CEW samples are showing ratios from origins too far north of North America. We are skeptical because at the time we caught these moths, the environment was not suitable for CEW development at any stage.  Biologically speaking, it shouldn't be possible for these individuals to complete a life cycle within the month or so before the capture date, nor should it have been possible for these individuals, assuming they overwintered, to have emerged, as in both scenarios, the temperature requirements had not been reached in the upper latitudes. We also pondered if something could be wrong with our samples and/or calibration samples, though comparing those to the GNIP measurand trends, we don't suspect an issue such as contamination (both northern-originated CEW and the northern areas have greater negative ratios <-100). Also, I am unaware of a type of contaminant that would cause a greater depletion of deuterium/increase of heavy H. The last explanation we thought of was a labeling error, but that would've had to be a repeated error across different batches at different times. So since every other explanation we’ve thought of is improbable, we thought there could be something else we are unaware of. Maybe others have encountered similar results, and there is an explanation beyond that these individuals actually have natal origins from the far northern regions, as they appear?

So my questions more concisely are:

All samples were kept in freezers and if caught on the same day within a trap in the same bag, what contaminant or process could occur that depletes light hydrogen in a couple of individuals within a batch of moths?

Could there be a statistical error behind the results that assign a sample's origin to these northern regions?

As of now, we have assumed no errors, but we wanted to be sure we consider alternative explanations before fully accepting the results.

I’ve attached the assignment maps in question. Let me know if I should clarify anything.

A CEW was caught in New Jersey, with the most likely origin from areas that have not reached the temperature requirement.

A CEW was caught in New York with extreme northern origins, where temperature requirements were also too low

Three other CEWs caught the same week were all from different locations, each with likely origins from far northern Canada. The temperature trends and resource availability make this unlikely.

Bukola

The boundaries in `prepsources()` are only there to filter out some location in the data.
When you plot the isoscape, it thus does not use the coordinate boundaries you fixed in `prepsources()` but it uses the one from the raster you give to `isoscape()`.
So you need to change the coordinates of this raster using the arguments in `get_elev()` (if you are using that) or in `prepraster()`.

Silly example (since based on land data from Germany):
library(IsoriX)
GNIPDataDEagg <- prepsources(data = GNIPDataDE, long_min = 0, long_max = 90)
GermanFit <- isofit(data = GNIPDataDEagg)

elev <- getelev(file = "~/elevation_world_z5.tif",
                z = 5,

                long_min = -66, long_max = -63,
                lat_min = -44, lat_max = -41)

raster <- prepraster(raster = terra::rast(elev))
GermanScape <- isoscape(raster = raster, isofit = GermanFit)
plot(GermanScape, mask = list(mask = NULL))

>
> Following this, when I use the code for the calibration samples I read the following warning: Note: extrapolation issuesOut of your 121 calibration samples, * 66 correspond to locations outside the area covered by the measurements you used to build your isoscape. --> These cases correspond to extrapolation during the calibration step, which could impede the reliability of your assignments.
> I finf it odd because all my samples come from the same geographic points but are from different animal nature: for the base raster I use zooplankton and for calibration phytoplankton samples.

I find it odd as well, but perhaps it is because the data are exactly on top of each others so perhaps numerical noise creates the issue.
It would be useful for me to know. The underlying code is this:
    coord_points <- isofit$info_fit$data[, c("long", "lat")]
    points_contour <- grDevices::chull(coord_points)
    coord_contour <- coord_points[c(points_contour, points_contour[1]), ]
    points_obj <- terra::vect(x = as.data.frame(data[, c("long", "lat")]), geom = c("long", "lat"), crs = "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84")
    contour_obj <- terra::vect(x = as.matrix(coord_contour[, c("long", "lat")]), type = "polygons", crs = "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84")
    points_out <- !terra::is.related(points_obj, contour_obj, "within")
    sum(points_out) # number of calib point outside the range

So you can test what happens after replacing `isofit$info_fit$data` (line 1) with your source dataset and `data` (line 4) by your calibration dataset.
You should get 66 as an output.
You can then visualise the situation using this:

plot(points_obj)
plot(contour_obj, add =TRUE)

> Following to the assignment part, in my case skin dolphin samples, all of them have a p- value greater than 0.05. As I understand none of them could be assigned to the geographic area I defined, showing it like this:
>

I guess you meant "all of them have a p- value lower than 0.05".
I think there could be a problem with the calibration (and/or with the isoscape model).
So please check the points extrapolation issue first and show us the calibration plot.
++

> I was wondering if you can help me with this. In any case I am very greatful for your help for all the IsoriX community.
>
> Kind regards,
> Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bukola,
Sorry for the delay, this is a busy season for me...
So if there is a mismatch between you expectation and what IsoriX predicts, the main possibilities are:
- there is a problem with the data
- there is a problem with the data preparation
- there is a problem with the calibration model or its fit
- there is a problem with the isoscape model or its fit
Since the issue often stem from the calibration step, could you first show us the calibration fits (pictures) for 2023 and 2024 separately?
++

Biologically speaking, it shouldn't be possible for these individuals to complete a life cycle within the month or so before the capture date, nor should it have been possible for these individuals, assuming they overwintered, to have emerged, as in both scenarios, the temperature requirements had not been reached in the upper latitudes. The last explanation we thought of was a labeling error, but that would've had to be a repeated error across different batches at different times.
